To abhor something means to feel a deep, intense hatred or disgust toward it — so strong that it almost feels like a physical reaction of revulsion. It is not just disliking something. It is finding something so offensive, wrong, or repulsive that your whole being rejects it.

Think of it this way: you might dislike loud music at midnight. You might hate being stuck in traffic. But you abhor something that strikes you as deeply wrong, cruel, or morally repulsive — like injustice, cruelty, or dishonesty.

"Abhor" sits at the extreme end of a scale of negative feelings:

Dislike → Hate → Detest → Abhor / Loathe

It is one of the strongest words in English for expressing negative feeling. When someone says they abhor something, they are not exaggerating for effect — the word itself already carries that extreme weight.
The moral dimension — what makes "abhor" special

This is the key detail that separates "abhor" from simply saying "I hate this."

When you abhor something, it is almost always because it violates your values, ethics, or sense of right and wrong — not just your personal taste. It carries a sense of moral outrage alongside the disgust.

For example:

  • You might hate the taste of broccoli. But you would not say you abhor broccoli, because that would be strange — abhor implies a deeper, moral kind of rejection.
  • You would say you abhor racism, cruelty to animals, or corruption — because these things feel fundamentally wrong, not just unpleasant.

This moral weight is what gives the word its power.

"Abhor" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — something that you abhor. You cannot just say "she abhors." You must say what she abhors.

The structure is always: subject + abhor + object

Here are the forms of the verb:

  • I / you / we / they abhor
  • He / she / it abhors
  • Past tense: abhorred (note: the 'r' is doubled — abhorred, not abhored)
  • Present participle: abhorring (again, double 'r')

"She abhors violence in any form — she cannot even watch action movies."
→ She finds violence so repulsive that she rejects it completely.

"He abhorred the way the prisoners were treated."
→ In the past, he felt deep moral disgust at this treatment.

"Most decent people abhor cruelty."
→ Cruelty is morally repulsive to them.

"The teacher abhors dishonesty more than anything else."
→ Dishonesty offends her values deeply and profoundly.

"They abhorred the idea of leaving anyone behind."
→ The very thought of it was repulsive and unacceptable to them.
What kinds of things do people abhor?

In real usage, "abhor" almost always appears with things that are considered morally wrong or deeply repulsive:

Abhor violence. Abhor cruelty. Abhor injustice. Abhor corruption. Abhor hypocrisy. Abhor the thought of something. Abhor racism.

You will rarely see it used for trivial personal preferences. If someone uses "abhor" about something small (like a food), it is usually done with humour or exaggeration — and the joke works precisely because the word is so serious and heavy.
Register — when and where is this word used?

"Abhor" is a formal word. You are far more likely to read it in a novel, a speech, a news article, or a formal essay than to hear it in everyday casual conversation. In informal speech, people tend to say "I hate" or "I can't stand" or "I detest." But in writing, or when someone wants to express something with weight and gravity, "abhor" is the word they reach for.
One-line summary to anchor it in your memory
To abhor something = to hate it so deeply, and find it so morally repulsive, that your whole being rejects it.
